item.title: Fixing Floating Point Comparison Issues: When Is '==' Unreliable in Code
item.description:
“Fixing Floating Point Comparison Issues: When Is ‘==’ Unreliable in Code”

Why does using the standard equality operator (==) often lead to unexpected results when comparing floating-point numbers like sectionID and currentSectionID in code? This behavior stems from the fundamental way computers store non-integer decimal values, following standards like IEEE 754.

Most decimal fractions (like 0.1 or 0.3) cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point format. Instead, the system stores a very close approximation. This slight deviation, known as rounding error or precision loss during the decimal-to-binary conversion, means two values that should be mathematically identical might possess slightly different internal binary representations.

item.title: Python Mutability Explained: Mutable vs Immutable Objects
item.description:
“Python Mutability Explained: Mutable vs Immutable Objects”

In Python, the concept of mutability is fundamental to how objects behave and how data is manipulated. Understanding the difference between mutable and immutable objects can prevent unexpected behavior and lead to more robust code.

At its core, mutability refers to whether an object’s state can be changed after it’s created.

  • Mutable Objects: These objects can be modified “in place” after they are created. Changes made to a mutable object through one variable will be reflected when accessed through another variable referencing the same object.
  • Immutable Objects: These objects cannot be changed after creation. Any operation that appears to modify an immutable object actually creates a new object with the desired changes, and the original object remains unaltered.

How Do Operations Like += Work?

You might see operations like x = 5.0 followed by x += 7.0, which results in 12.0. This might seem like x is being mutated. However, for immutable types like floats and strings, this operation creates a new object. The variable x is then reassigned to refer to this new object.

item.title: value vs reference types explained
item.description:
“value vs reference types explained”

The distinction between value types and reference types is fundamental to how data is stored and manipulated in memory within many programming languages, such as C#, Java, and Python. Understanding this difference is key to predicting how your code will behave, especially when passing variables to functions or assigning one variable to another.

Value Types:

  • Direct Data Storage: Value types directly contain their data. When you declare a variable of a value type, memory is allocated to hold the actual value itself.
  • Stack Allocation (Often): Typically, value types are stored on the stack. The stack is a region of memory that operates on a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle, making it efficient for managing local variables and function call information.
  • Copy on Assignment/Passing: When you assign a value type variable to another, or pass it to a function, a complete copy of the value is created. Changes made to the copy do not affect the original.
